newsitem.title: UK: Dollar/yen lurches lower on mounting trade worries.
newsitem.headline: Dollar/yen lurches lower on mounting trade worries.

text.p: The dollar lurched to a near-seven-month low against the yen as concern that the U.S. will take issue with Japan's widening trade surplus grew before next week's meeting of the world's largest industrial nations.
U.S. Deputy Secretary Lawrence Summers triggered the slump in the dollar after he said Wednesday Japan should avoid running up external surpluses that would hurt global growth.
His comments hit home, coming in the wake of a report which showed Japan's current account and trade surplus surging in April. They also eclipsed his call Tuesday for a strong dollar.

It was left to senior Japanese officials to mount a damage limitation exercise. Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka warned Japan would act to combat excessive currency swings while Bank of Japan Governor Yasuo Matsushita called for more stability.

Traders are inclined to disregard the Japanese authorities urgings, though, given they haven't managed to stop the dollar tumbling over 13 percent from a four-and-a-half-year high of 127.46 in little more than a month.
"The market wants to be short of dollar/yen despite the clear wishes of the Japanese authorities," said Nick Parsons, the currency strategist at Paribas Capital Markets.
"What's ironic is that only six weeks ago they were trying to buy it at 127 in the face of Japanese concern."

The dollar fell to 110.62 yen, its weakest since November 18, 1996. It was quoted at 111.28/38 yen at 1045 GMT from 112.43/53 late Tuesday in Europe. Mark/yen tumbled to 64.69 yen, its weakest since August 1995 and was last at 64.91/94 from 65.41/44 Wednesday. Dollar/mark was at 1.7145/55 from 1.7188/93 Tuesday.

The dollar's 60 percent rebound from the post-World-War-II low of 79.76 it set in April 1995 has boosted Japanese exporters' competitiveness against their U.S. rivals and fuelled an increase in Japan's trade surpluses.
A report today showed Japan's current account surplus surged 92.7 percent in April from a year earlier while its trade surplus climbed 90.9 percent.

While Mitsuzuka said Japan's trade and services surplus was unlikely to rise significantly in the medium term, he also said the surpluses were likely to be topic of discussion when Group of Seven leading industrial nations meet in Denver on June 20-22. Traders don't expect an easing of U.S. trade pressure soon.
"The U.S. seems to be stepping up the war of words and it looks like we are going to test the 110 (yen) levels," said Steve Hannah, the director of research at IBJ International.

Currencies may join trade on the G-7's agenda if the dollar continues to ratchet lower. The G-7 have welcomed the correction of 1995's currency misalignments, and said at their two meetings earlier this year that they would now prefer exchange rates to be more stable.

Traders, who make more money out of volatility, have preferred to test the limits of G-7 tolerance -- on the dollar's upside in May and now on its downside. Dollar/yen risk reversal, the difference in the implied volatility of calls relative to puts, is up at 2.0/2.4 percent, its highest since August 1995 when central banks bought dollars in concert to stem its slide.
Such levels are "usually a good indicator that central bank intervention is due," said Ian Gromme, a foreign-exchange options trader at ABN Amro.

The Bank for International Settlements said Monday that German and U.S. monetary authorities had not intervened in the currency markets in 1996 or in the first quarter of 1997. It also said the Bank of Japan did not appear to have intervened in the past year.
The success with which the authorities have manipulated the direction of the dollar's moves without spending any money should make traders wary of taking them on, analysts said.
"To bet against the Japanese authorities on the dollar's direction is risky, if not mad," said Parsons at Paribas.
Investors who have been running long yen positions are also not expecting the dollar's slide to keep going and may offer the U.S. currency some support by moving to lock in gains.

"We are moderately overweight of yen and not inclined to do anything until next week," said Ian Winship, a fund manager at Scottish Amicable Investment Managers. "But if Europe settles down, and if dollar/yen is still here at that point, we'll probably take some profits." -London newsroom +44 171 542 6284
